L0: # Compositional May-Must Program Analysis: Unleashing the Power of Alternation
L1: 
L2:   * Patrice Godefroid ,
L3:   * 【0†Aditya Nori】 ,
L4:   * 【1†Sriram Rajamani】 ,
L5:   * Sai Deep Tetali
L6: 
L7: Principles of Programming Languages (POPL) | January 2010
L8: 
L9: Published by Association for Computing Machinery, Inc.
L10: 
L11: 【2†Download BibTex】
L12: Program analysis tools typically compute two types of information: (1) may information that is true of all program executions and is used to prove the absence of bugs in the program, and (2) must information that is true of some program executions and is used to prove the existence of bugs in the program. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, dubbed SMASH, which computes both may and must information compositionally.
L13: At each procedure boundary, may and must information is represented and stored as may and must summaries, respectively. Those summaries are computed in a demand-driven manner and possibly using summaries of the opposite type. We have implemented SMASH using predicate abstraction (as in SLAM) for the may part and using dynamic test generation (as in DART) for the must part.
L14: Results of experiments with 69 Microsoft Windows Vista device drivers show that SMASH can significantly outperform may-only, must-only and non-compositional may-must algorithms. Indeed, our empirical results indicate that most complex code fragments in large programs are actually often either easy to prove irrelevant to the specific property of interest using may analysis or easy to traverse using directed testing.
L15: The fine-grained coupling and alternation of may (universal) and must (existential) summaries allows SMASH to easily navigate through these code fragments while traditional may-only, must-only or noncompositional may-must algorithms are stuck in their specific analyses.

L7@P0: Abstract. The idea to use simulations (or refinements) as a compositional abstraction device is well-known, both in untimed and timed settings, and has already been studied theoretically and practically in many
L8@P0: papers during the last three decades. Nevertheless, existing approaches
L9@P0: do not handle two fundamental modeling concepts which, for instance,
L10@P0: are frequently used in the popular Uppaal model checker: (1) a parallel
L11@P0: composition operator that supports communication via shared variables
L12@P0: as well as synchronization of actions, and (2) committed locations. In
L13@P0: this paper, we describe a framework for compositional abstraction based
L14@P0: on simulation relations that does support both concepts, and that is
L15@P0: suitable for Uppaal. Our approach is very general and the only essential
L16@P0: restriction is that the guards of input transitions do not depend on external variables. We have applied our compositional framework to verify
L17@P0: the Zeroconf protocol for an arbitrary number of hosts.
L18@P0: 1 Introduction
L19@P0: In this paper, we describe a framework for compositional abstraction based on
L20@P0: simulation relations that is suitable for the Uppaal model checker [4]. The
L21@P0: idea to use simulations (or refinements) as a compositional abstraction device
L22@P0: is well-known, both in untimed and timed settings, and has already been studied theoretically and practically in many papers during the last three decades,
L23@P0: see for instance [28,23,19,26,22,20,1,27,16,17,14,12,21]. Nevertheless, when we
L24@P0: attempted to apply these existing approaches to fight state space explosions in
L25@P0: a model of an industrial protocol [13], we ran into the problem that these approaches do not handle two fundamental modeling concepts that are frequently
L26@P0: used in Uppaal.
L27@P0: The first concept is a parallel composition operator that supports communication via both shared variables and synchronization of actions. Models for
L28@P0: reactive systems typically either support communication via shared variables
L29@P0: (TLA [24], Reactive Modules [3], etc), or communication via synchronization of
L30@P0: actions (CCS [29], I/O automata [26], etc). We are only aware of two studies of
L31@P0: compositionality in which the two types of communication are combined [25,17].
L32@P0: ? Research supported by NWO/EW project 612.000.103 Fault-tolerant Real-time Algorithms Analyzed Incrementally (FRAAI) and DFG/NWO bilateral cooperation
L33@P0-1: project Validation of Stochastic Systems (VOSS2).It is well known that both types of communication can be defined in terms of
L34@P1: each other. A shared variable can be modeled as a separate process/automaton
L35@P1: that communicates with its environment via read/write synchronization actions.
L36@P1: However, in this approach the evaluation of, for instance, an integer expression
L37@P1: may involve a sequence of interactions with shared variable automata. This blows
L38@P1: up the state space and makes it more difficult to understand the model. Conversely, synchronization of actions can be modeled in a shared variable setting
L39@P1: using some auxiliary flag variables and handshake transitions of the synchronizing automata. But again this blows up the state space and makes it harder to
L40@P1: understand the model. The Uppaal model checker supports both shared variables and synchronization of actions, and this feature is extremely helpful for
L41@P1: building tractable models of complex systems.
L42@P1: When combining shared variables and synchronization of actions, one has to
L43@P1: deal with the scenario, illustrated in Figure 1, in which the transitions involved
L44@P1: in a synchronization assign different values to a shared variable. One simple

L50@P1: (but restrictive) approach, pursued in [25], is to impose syntactic conditions
L51@P1: which ensure that the scenario does not occur: for each shared variable only
L52@P1: one automaton gets write permission, and the other automata may read the
L53@P1: variable but not assign a new value to it. A slightly more general approach is
L54@P1: taken in [17], where the variables of each automaton are classified as readable
L55@P1: and/or writable. Two automata may share writable variables, but in this case
L56@P1: a synchronizing transition may only occur if both automata assign the same

L96@P2: In Uppaal, a synchronization may only occur if the guards of both transitions
L97@P2: hold, and only if this is the case the assignments are carried out. This means that
L98@P2: if we add a guard v 6= 1 to the rightmost transition in Figure 1, synchronization
L99@P2: will be possible starting from any state satisfying this predicate. In a semantics
L100@P2: with rule (1), however, synchronization will no longer be possible since after the
L101@P2: assignment on the output transitions has been performed, the guard of the input
L102@P2: transition no longer holds1. In order to rule out this scenario (which we have
L103@P2: never observed in practical applications), our approach imposes the restriction
L104@P2: that guards of input transitions do not refer to external (shared) variables.
L105@P2: The second modeling concept, which is not handled by any existing framework but needed for industrial applications, is the notion of a committed location.
L106@P2: In Uppaal, locations of a timed automata can be designated as committed. If one
L107@P2: automaton in a network of automata is in a committed location, time may not
L108@P2: progress and the next transition (if any) has to start from a committed location.
L109@P2: Committedness is useful to specify that certain transitions need to be executed
L110@P2: atomically without intervening transitions from other components. Also, excluding certain behavior with committed locations may lead to serious reductions in
L111@P2: the state space of a model [7]. In this paper, we present a compositional semantics for committedness. This is achieved by distinguishing, at the semantic
L112@P2: level, between committed and uncommitted transitions. Our rules for describing
L113@P2: committed locations involve negative antecedents and are similar to the rules
L114@P2: that have been proposed in the process algebra literature to describe priorities
L115@P2: [9,11,30,2]: a component may only perform a uncommitted τ -transition if other
L116@P2: components may not perform a committed transition. Although there are some
L117@P2: subtle differences at the technical level, basically our results show that one may
L118@P2: view committedness as a form of priority.
L119@P2: We define the semantics of timed automata in terms of timed transition systems (TTSs). These are labeled transition systems (LTSs) equipped with a bit
L120@P2: of additional structure to capture relevant information about state variables,
L121@P2: committedness of transitions, and real-time behavior. On TTSs we define the
L122@P2: operations of parallel composition and a CCS style restriction operator. An important sanity check for our definitions is that, for any network of timed automata, the (noncompositional) Uppaal semantics (as defined in the Uppaal
L123@P2: 4.0 help menu) is isomorphic to the (compositional) semantics obtained by associating TTSs to the timed automata in the network, composing these TTSs
L124@P2: in parallel, applying a restriction operator, and then considering the underlying
L125@P2: LTS. That is, if N = hA1, . . . , Ani is a network of timed automata then
L126@P2: LTS(N ) ∼= LTS((TTS(A1)k · · · kTTS(An))\C).
L127@P2: A key lemma needed to prove this result is associativity of parallel composition.

L132@P3: These induce a behavioral preorder  that is somewhere in between strong and

L139@P3: Section 2 introduces timed transition systems. In Section 3, we define timed
L140@P3: step simulations and establish that the induced preorder is compositional. Section 4 presents networks of timed automata and defines their semantics both noncompositionally (as in Uppaal) and compositionally in terms of TTSs. Also, the
L141@P3: consistency of the two semantic definitions is established and we briefly discuss
L142@P3: the application of our framework. Finally, Section 5 discusses some extensions
L143@P3: and future research. An appendix summarizes some of the notational conventions
L144@P3: used in the paper.
L145@P3: 2 Timed Transition Systems
L146@P3: In this section, we introduce the semantic model of timed transitions systems
L147@P3: (TTSs). Basically, a TTS is a labeled transition system equipped with a bit of additional structure to support shared variables and committed transitions: states
L148@P3: are defined as valuations of variables, and transitions may be committed, which
L149@P3: gives them a certain priority in a parallel composition. TTSs can be placed in
L150@P3: parallel and may communicate by means of shared variables and synchronization
L151@P3: of actions. Like in CCS [29], two transitions may synchronize when their actions
L152@P3: are complementary, leading to an internal transition in the composition.
L153@P3: Just to fix notation, we first recall the definition of a labeled transition system
L154@P3: in Section 2.1. Since we consider systems that communicate via shared variables,
L155@P3: we find it convenient to model states as functions that map state variables to values in their domain. Section 2.2 introduces a basic vocabulary for overriding and
L156@P3: updating of functions that we need to describe shared variable communication.
L157@P3: After these preliminaries, Section 2.3 presents the definition of a timed transition system. Next, Section 2.4 defines the operations of parallel composition and
L158@P3: restriction, and establishes some key properties of these operations, in particular
L159@P3: associativity of parallel composition. Finally, Section 2.5 discusses in some more
L160@P3: detail why in our approach committedness is an attribute of transitions rather
L161@P3: than states.

L276@P6: The state variables of a TTS are partitioned into external and internal variables. Internal variables may only be updated by the TTS itself and not by its
L277@P6: environment. This in contrast to external variables, which may be updated by
L278@P6: both the TTS and its environment. A new element in our definition of a TTS is
L279@P6: that transitions are classified as either committed or uncommitted. Committed
L280@P6: transitions have priority over time-passage transitions and over internal transitions that are not committed. Interestingly, whereas in Uppaal committedness
L281@P6: is an attribute of locations, it must be treated as an attribute of transitions in
L282@P6: order to obtain a compositional semantics. This issue will be further discussed
L283@P6: in Section 2.5.
